mappings.note: Full bench description of separating black ink dyes: spot near the bottom, paper dipped, differing rates of travel. LO-11's principle clause at three-mark length.

Diagram plus mechanism of centrifugation for heavy solids in a liquid. LO-13 is the only outcome naming centrifugation; the item never says filtration was tried, which is why the fine-particle clause of LO-13 is implied rather than stated.

Rebuts 'brass is a compound' by arguing it is a homogeneous mixture with variable composition whose metals keep their properties -- LO-6's alloy case plus its 'why a solution is homogeneous' reasoning turned on a solid.

Two genuinely separate halves: the definition of a saturated solution is LO-8, and the step-by-step purification of copper sulfate by crystallisation is LO-9. Neither half can carry the other, so both are cited.
Coagulation in a water-treatment plant, with alum clumping fine river silt. LO-13's coagulation clause, the long-form version of the alum MCQs.
Labelled sublimation setup for camphor and sand, plus what happens to the camphor on heating -- both clauses of LO-12. Two components only, so LO-16 does not apply.
Defines dispersed phase and dispersion medium and then applies both to milk -- LO-15's naming clause. No Tyndall test and no size band, so it stays off LO-14.

Doubling the solute in a fixed volume doubles the concentration, and the consequences follow from that. LO-7 is the concentration outcome; the reasoning is proportional rather than a worked sum, which is why this sits at the looser end of the LO-7 family alongside the ORS item.
Why more solute dissolves in hot water, argued from molecular energy -- LO-8's 'how solubility changes with temperature'. No saturated solution is cooled and no crystals form, so not LO-9.
Identifies simple distillation from the diagram and names the boiling-point difference as the enabling property -- LO-10. The apparatus is only the route to the property question.

POOR FIT, third instance of the same gap. The term defined is mass by VOLUME percentage, which LO-7 does not list (it names mass by mass and volume by volume only). Cited as nearest concentration code; % m/V has no outcome in curriculum 82.

Explains fractional distillation and why refineries need it rather than simple distillation -- LO-10 carries both methods and the choice between them, so this is squarely its 'states when each is the appropriate method' clause.

Rebuts the claim that every solid's solubility rises identically with temperature, by pointing at differing curve gradients -- LO-8's curve-reading clause used to argue rather than to extract a number.

Before-and-after diagram of a blood tube, explained by the outward force driving cells down. LO-13's centrifugation clause. Blood's colloidal nature is background here; the assessed content is what the spin does, not how blood is classified, which is what separates this from the LO-14 blood items.
Defines % v/v and states its formula -- LO-7 names volume by volume explicitly, so unlike its % m/V neighbours this one sits inside the outcome rather than beside it.

Oil-in-water versus water-in-oil, each labelled by dispersed phase and medium with an example -- LO-15's emulsion and naming clauses together. The frame gives emulsions no outcome of their own, so the whole emulsion family lands here.

The visible beam in a dark room is dust and smoke scattering light -- LO-15. Same outcome as the hazy-city and forest-sunbeam items; all three are the Tyndall effect observed outside the lab and the frame offers no way to distinguish them.

Compares curve steepness for two compounds and predicts what happens as one cools -- LO-8's curve reading. Family rule: the deposit on cooling is inferred from the curve, so it stays on LO-8 rather than moving to LO-9.

Molten metals cooling into a uniform solid, and why physical methods cannot pull them apart -- LO-6's alloy clause and its homogeneity argument. Nothing here is a separation technique to be selected, so it stays under C1.2.

The negative case for the separating funnel: acetone and alcohol are miscible so no layers form. That is LO-11's justification clause used to rule the method OUT. Not LO-10, because the item asks what fails, not what to use instead.

POOR FIT and vaguely worded. Half the answer is kidneys filtering blood, which no outcome in this frame covers, and half is municipal sewage treatment, which is LO-13's coagulation and settling. LO-13 plus the competency is the honest ceiling; stretching a single LO over the biological half would misrepresent it.

Asks why water or alcohol is able to carry the pigments up the paper -- this is the clearest item in the chapter on LO-11's second clause, 'the basis on which a solvent is chosen', rather than on the mechanism of the run.

Copper sulfate purification with a cooling diagram, then why crystallisation beats evaporation to dryness -- both parts are LO-9's principle and its purity consequence. The saturated solution is a step, not the assessed idea, so LO-8 is not added here as it was for item S104, which defines the term outright.
Part (c) -- would alcohol instead of water change the pattern -- is directly LO-11's solvent-choice clause, and parts (a) and (b) are its principle clause. One outcome covers the whole item.

Part (a) defines sublimation and deposition (LO-12); part (b) asks for an ordered three-component separation of camphor, sand and salt (LO-16). Both cited because the definition half would be lost under LO-16 alone.
